issues.issue: An agreement to "confer in good faith to discuss the scope and timing of discovery" imposes no obligation to agree and no standard by which good faith is measured. The party named, "MGF Holdings, Limited," is also not the entity named elsewhere in the Agreement ("MGF Sourcing Holdings, Limited").

The mutual duty to keep Detailed Delivery Schedule pricing confidential cannot be squared with section 7, which requires the Debtors to file a revised Exhibit A (the Detailed Delivery Schedule) with the Settlement Motion on the public docket. Whether that filing is a breach or is excused depends on reading the two provisions together.

The disclosing party must take "all reasonable actions necessary" to obtain a protective order or seal "to the extent possible," two open-ended qualifiers with no benchmark and no consequence if the court refuses. It is also silent on whether disclosure may proceed when sealing fails.

The permitted disclosure runs only to the Debtors and is conditioned on "the recipient agrees to keep such information confidential," with no stated form of agreement and no remedy against a recipient such as the term loan lenders (Sycamore affiliates) who do not agree. The asymmetry with MGF's obligations under the preceding sentence is left unexplained.

The cooperation duty turns on "minor delays," "significant deliveries" and whether a delay "materially impact[s]" each party's operations — none defined and each the probable subject of dispute. The chargeback and rejection carve-outs then attach to "any such above described minor delays," importing the same undefined threshold into a substantive bar.

The assistance obligation is qualified twice over — "reasonable business efforts, whenever possible" — with no benchmark for either, and no definition of when a party "need[s] assistance." Reasonable advance notice is likewise left unquantified.

The parties must "cooperate in good faith to resolve any such discrepancies" but the provision supplies no mechanism or tiebreaker if they cannot agree, and orders are only removed where the parties "mutually agree (in writing)." A discrepancy in the Detailed Delivery Schedule therefore has no contractual resolution path.

The bar on public announcements without mutual written consent has no exception for statements required by law, securities rules or bankruptcy court filings, unlike the legal-process exception given to pricing information in section 8(c). Its reach over "any commentary" about the parties is also unbounded in time and subject matter.

The clause provides only that a waiver is not a waiver of "any other provision or condition," saying nothing about whether a waiver of a given provision operates as to future breaches of that same provision. The omission is the classic gap in a non-waiver clause.

The integration clause declares the entire agreement to be this Agreement "together with ... the Sourcing Agreement as modified hereby," which has to be reconciled with section 8(m) and section 6 as to which Sourcing Agreement terms (the termination fee, shortfall and rebate provisions, section 4(b)(ii)) survive. Its "subject matter herein" limitation leaves the superseded scope uncertain.

Amendments adverse "to the interests of the lenders party to the DIP Financing" require consent of non-parties, with no standard for what is adverse and no means of determining who "any required lenders" are. Whether an amendment is effective thus depends on an undefined judgment about third-party interests.

The statement that nothing in the Agreement modifies the DIP Financing has to be reconciled with section 3, whose carve-outs (a)-(c) make the consequences of a DIP Event of Default turn on MGF's conduct and on cure or waiver periods of the parties' own devising. Which instrument governs the effect of a DIP default on trade terms is open.

"The preceding sentence" has an ambiguous antecedent in a paragraph containing four long sentences covering integration, consideration, amendments and DIP Financing. What exactly must be written into the Settlement Order is therefore uncertain.

The binding list enumerates purchasers, liquidation agents, reorganized Debtors and chapter 11 or 7 trustees and then adds the catch-all "any other successor to the Debtors," inviting an ejusdem generis argument about whether, e.g., a plan administrator or creditor trust is covered. "Successor" is itself undefined in the Agreement.

"a provision to such effect" does not specify the content, scope or wording the Settlement Order must contain, and duplicates the similar directive in section 8(g). Whether an order lacking such a provision breaches the Agreement or merely fails the section 7 condition is unaddressed.

"all things reasonably necessary, or as may be reasonably requested" to carry out the "purposes and intent" of the Agreement supplies no boundary on what can be demanded. The grammatical slip "by other party" leaves the obligee unidentified.

The Agreement's units are numbered paragraphs with lettered subsections, and internal cross-references are to lowercase "section 3" and to "clause (a)" and "this paragraph," so a rule governing only "Section" and "Sections" does not reach the references actually used. The mismatch leaves the interpretive rule without application to most cross-references.

New York law is chosen without regard to conflicts principles, yet section 5(e) has the parties waive California Civil Code Section 1542 — a statute that can have no application under the chosen law. A court could be asked which provision governs the effect of the unknown-claims waiver.

"Except as amended by this Agreement, the Sourcing Agreement remains in full force and effect until terminated in accordance with this Agreement" must be read against section 6, which terminates the Sourcing Agreement automatically on final delivery and payment and kills specified provisions on finality of the Settlement Order, and against section 7, which can void this Agreement entirely. What survives, and when, is determined only by reading the instrument as a whole.
